newsitem.title: CHINA: Israel's Levy plays down settlement fears.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Levy plays down settlement fears.

text.p: Visiting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Wednesday played down concerns over plans for new Jewish settlements in East Jerusalem, and said there was no need for outsiders arbiters each time the peace process hit snags.
"We have a solid and good relationship with Palestinian authorities," he told reporters in the Chinese capital.

Replying to reporters' questions about Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's call to Europe and the United States to save the Middle East peace process, he said: "There is no reason to invite an outside arbiter every time we have a difference.
"Arafat and I have decided that issues must be discussed -- the way of violence must be excluded," he said.

The U.N. Security Council has expressed concern over Israeli settlement plans in East Jerusalem, particularly those to build 6,500 homes on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, called Har Homa by Israel and Jabal Abu-Ghneim by Palestinians.
Arafat has said such settlements were aimed at making demographic changes and went against the peace process.
However, Levy said the settlements were not a violation of any Middle East peace accords.
"This does not breach any sort of agreement," he said. "Jews will build in Jerusalem and Arabs will build. It must be co-existence."
The foreign minister characterised Israel as proceeding cautiously in its settlements policies.
"I hope we will reach an agreement," he said. "There is no alternative to the peace process."
Levy, who met senior Chinese officials including President Jiang Zemin during his three-day stay, said Beijing expressed opposition to violence inspired by religious fundamentalism.
Israel and China shared similar views on the issue, he said.

China has been hit by periodic separatist violence in its mainly Moslem, western region of Xinjiang. Beijing maintains that outside agitators, some of them preaching radical religious doctrines, are behind the violence.
Three bombs planted in buses blew up in the Xinjiang capital of Urumqi on Tuesday, killing at least four people and wounding dozens, according to residents and officials.
